newsitem.title: JAPAN: Isuzu sees no reduction at Japan engine plant.
newsitem.headline: Isuzu sees no reduction at Japan engine plant.

text.p: Isuzu Motors Ltd president Kazuhira Seki said on Thursday he expects no reduction in output at the company's Tomakomai engine plant on Japan's northern island of Hokkaido as a result of a planned Polish engine plant.

"Planned output volume in Poland is nearly equal to the volume of diesel engines supplied to Adam Opel from our Hokkaido plant. But we decided to build the engine plant in Poland because we are confident we will maintain production at both plants," Seki told a news conference.
"Isuzu is planning to expand engine supplies to other makers on an original equipment manufacturing basis (OEM), Seki added.
Isuzu's Tomakomai plant now supplies some 180,000 diesel engines for use in Opel cars. Adam Opel AG is the German unit of General Motors Corp (GM). GM owns 37.4 percent of Isuzu.

Isuzu announced Thursday that it will ask permission to build a diesel engine plant in Katowice Province to start production by the summer of 1999 with an annual output of 200,000 in 1999, and 300,000 in 2000.
The engines to be produced by the Polish plant will be mainly supplied to GM's group companies such as Opel.
"Demand for diesel engines is sure to expand further in the future...in view of the advantages in fuel economy and emissions, and progress on reducing engine noise and vibration," Seki said.

Itsuo Sugihara, an Isuzu managing director in charge of product planning and vehicle engineering, said that Isuzu is in talks with other automakers on supplying their Polish-made diesel engines but he refused to identify them.
